note: Sets out the interface problems between the AI Act and the medical device regulations, which is the first thing to resolve in a clinical audit.
title: Risk-adjusted conformity assessment of AI systems in healthcare: A scoping review
explain_beginner: The paper reviews 126 studies and reports about how the European Union checks whether healthcare AI is safe and compliant. Medical AI must follow both medical device rules and the AI Act, and the review finds this creates overlap and confusion. It also notes that many medical AI tools are treated as high risk, that systems which keep learning are hard to certify once and forget, and that monitoring after release is unclear. The authors say the legal framework is broad, but practical application is still debated. This matters because unclear duties could leave doctors responsible for AI performance they cannot easily verify.
explain_business: For healthcare organizations and AI vendors, this review suggests that EU rules for medical AI are broad but not yet easy to apply consistently. The main practical issue is the overlap between the AI Act and medical device rules, plus uncertainty about how to monitor AI that changes after deployment. The paper points to limited shared evidence measures, strained review bodies, and unclear responsibility for after market performance. Executives should treat regulatory strategy as ongoing lifecycle governance, not a one time approval. Decisions should include who monitors performance, who owns accountability, and how to gather evidence that regulators and clinicians can use to verify performance.
explain_practitioner: The authors did a scoping review following Arksey and O'Malley and Levac and colleagues, reported with PRISMA-ScR. They searched bibliographic databases and grey literature for EU-focused work on risk-based compliance checks for healthcare AI. After screening and full text review, they included 126 publications from January 2022 to October 2025 and used thematic synthesis. Key findings were recurring problems: unclear boundaries between the AI Act and MDR or IVDR, broad high risk classification, weak lifecycle governance for adaptive systems, principle to practice gaps, few shared evidence metrics, limited notified body capacity, and unresolved after market evidence and accountability questions. The framework is comprehensive but uneven in practice.
